name: Corrie ten Boom
title: Corrie ten Boom: an open house in the face of Nazi persecution
description: Corrie ten Boom and her family protected Jews during the Holocaust. A story documented by the USHMM and the museum in Haarlem.

sections.heading: The watch shop that became a refuge
paragraphs: The ten Boom family owned a watch shop in Haarlem. Corrie worked in that trade and took part in relief activities before the war. When Germany occupied the Netherlands in 1940, the danger to the Jewish population transformed the daily life of the city. The family eventually became part of a network of resistance and aid.

The family home came to hide persecuted people. The Haarlem museum dates the building and use of the hiding place to 1943, while the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum documents Corrie’s cooperation with the Dutch resistance. It was a shared effort: it required safe places, food, contacts and people willing to take risks.

sections.heading: Prison, loss and memory
paragraphs: Corrie was arrested in February 1944. She was held in Scheveningen prison and in the Vught and Ravensbrück camps. Several members of her family died in German custody. Her survival does not turn that experience into an adventure: it is part of the history of a persecution that destroyed whole families and communities.

After the war, Corrie spoke publicly about her faith and what she had lived through. The Hiding Place, published in 1971, spread her memoirs. Yad Vashem recognized her as Righteous Among the Nations in 1967. The museum and the USHMM make it possible to distinguish documented facts from details that belong to her autobiographical testimony.

reflection: The parable of the good Samaritan, in Luke 10:25–37, makes us think of love of neighbor as a concrete responsibility. Protecting someone who is being persecuted may demand more than expressing good feelings. The ten Boom house reminds us that a table, a door and an everyday decision can become places of service.

The story also invites us to listen with respect to the memory of the Jewish victims. The suffering of the Holocaust deserves to be understood in its own gravity. A Christian reading of this story must be accompanied by a clear condemnation of antisemitism and a willingness to recognize and protect the dignity of others.
review_note: The popular figure of 800 rescues and uncorroborated miracle stories are avoided. The Holocaust is presented in its Jewish historical context.
